Dynamic Electricity Demand Forecasting for Smart Cities
Authored by: Manoj Chowdary

Duration: 120 mins
Level: Intermediate
Pre-requisite Skills: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly, Scikit-learn

Scenario

Power distribution networks in urban smart cities are increasingly under pressure to meet rising demand caused by varying factors including weather and seasonal behavior, as well as the daily routines of people. This project proposes the implementation of a deep learning system that forecasts short-term future demand at a neighborhood scale. The project’s vision is to achieve improved demand forecasting and efficient energy distribution and consumption by implementing demand-response measures in order to maintain a healthy and efficient smart grid.
User Story

As a energy consumption data analyst. My role involves acquisition, exploration, processing of data of smart meters, with the goal of training deep learning models for forecasting electricity demand at the neighborhood scale. Such forecasting is critical for grid optimisation, reducing energy waste, and optimising demand-response in peaking situations.

What this use case will teach you

  • Import and load a big smart meter data set from Kaggle.
  • Analyze the profile and quality of energy data.
  • do some initial analysis on the data to look for temporal/ seasonal and neighborhood consumption patterns.
  • Integrate external weather data aligned by timestamp.
  • Engineer a set of temporal, lag, roll up, weather and feature based time series forecasting models.
  • Build deep learning models for forcasting enegey consumption using the features added.
  • Use the models for predecting future engery consumption based on weather and sevral other factors.

Introduction

Accuracy in electricity demand forecasting is crucial for the proper management of future smart grid operations. Previous models that utilized static time series properties such as historical consumption (for example, ARIMA and exponential smoothing) have struggled to generalize due to inherently complex temporal relationships found within energy consumption data. Recent deep learning models, such as LSTMs, CNN-LSTMs, and Transformers, are capable of better learning and modeling dynamic properties and thereby produce more accurate future predictions for electricity demand.

Dataset

In this notebook we will be using the UK Smart Meter Dataset from Kaggle. This dataset includes half-hourly readings from smart meters of around 5,500 households in London for the period 2011-2014.

**References:** - UK Smart Meter Dataset: Kaggle — Smart Meters in London

import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (14, 5)
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi'] = 100

print('All imports successful.')

Data Acquisition

We use the UK Smart Meter Dataset (London households).

The dataset contains :

  • Smart meter readings: Half hourly smart energy consumption in kWh for around 5500 households in London over a 3 year period, 2011-2014.
  • Weather data: hourly weather forecasts including temperature, humidity, wind, etc., from the Dark Sky API
  • Household metadata
  • ACORN group classifications (demographic/neighborhood)

• The readings go back roughly Nov 2011 to Feb 2014. so that is approximately 28 months which is sufficient to include at least two yearly cycles.
  • The majority of missing values are in energy_kwh (indicating some meter read failures). Most other fields, such as timestamp and household_id, are virtually complete.
  • `energy_kwh` is strongly right-skewed, with the mean only being around a fraction of a kWh per half hour, whereas the max is 4 time higher - this means that we will likely need to cap out the high-demand events or meter spikes that currently drive the max so far above normal usage.
Simply dropping rows with missing energy values which still leaves millions of usable records.
df_energy = df_energy.dropna(subset=['timestamp', 'energy_kwh', 'acorn_group'])

Aggregate to Neighborhood-Level Hourly Demand

The individual household data that we have is noisy, so we aggregate to the ACORN group level (neighborhood proxy) for the more stable forecasting target. This is done on an hourly basis.

q99 = df_energy['energy_kwh'].quantile(0.99)
df_energy = df_energy[(df_energy['energy_kwh'] >= 0) & (df_energy['energy_kwh'] <= q99)]

df_energy['hour'] = df_energy['timestamp'].dt.floor('h')

df_agg = (
    df_energy
    .groupby(['acorn_group', 'hour'])
    .agg(total_kwh=('energy_kwh', 'sum'),
         mean_kwh=('energy_kwh', 'mean'),
         num_meters=('household_id', 'nunique'))
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={'hour': 'timestamp', 'acorn_group': 'neighborhood'})
)

print(f"Aggregated dataset: {len(df_agg):,} rows")
print(f"Neighborhoods:      {df_agg['neighborhood'].nunique()}")
print(f"Time range:         {df_agg['timestamp'].min()}  →  {df_agg['timestamp'].max()}")
df_agg.head()

• We filtered the data at 99th percentile, which removes a small number of 'outliers'.
  • We aggregate per-household half-hourly readings up to hourly × ACORN group level (to strongly reduce noise and produce a compact panel data set to be modelled, as opposed to maintaining individual household time series).
  • This has reduced the dataset down to 39,485 rows and 2 Neighborhood groups. Time to pull the Summary Statistics.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
Overall Demand Distribution

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

axes[0].hist(df_agg['total_kwh'], bins=60, color='steelblue', edgecolor='white')
axes[0].set_title('Distribution of Hourly Demand')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Total kWh')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Frequency')

df_agg.boxplot(column='total_kwh', by='neighborhood', ax=axes[1], rot=45)
axes[1].set_title('Demand by Neighborhood')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Neighborhood')
axes[1].set_ylabel('kWh')
fig.suptitle('')

daily_total = df_agg.groupby('timestamp')['total_kwh'].sum().resample('D').sum()
axes[2].plot(daily_total.index, daily_total.values, color='darkgreen', linewidth=0.7)
axes[2].set_title('Daily Total Demand Over Time')
axes[2].set_xlabel('Date')
axes[2].set_ylabel('Total kWh')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

**Observations:**

- **Histogram (left):** Demand is highly right skewed with an upper tail.
- **Box plot (middle):** For richer ACORN groups (Affluent), the median demand is higher than Adversity groups, since their larger homes will contain more appliances.
- **Time series (right):** Daily total demand over time shows clear yearly seasonality with repeat patterns in each year of the data set with very high demand in the winter months.
Temporal Patterns — Hour of Day, Day of Week, Month

df_agg['hour_of_day'] = df_agg['timestamp'].dt.hour
df_agg['day_of_week'] = df_agg['timestamp'].dt.dayofweek
df_agg['month']       = df_agg['timestamp'].dt.month

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(20, 5))

df_agg.groupby('hour_of_day')['total_kwh'].mean().plot(
    kind='bar', ax=axes[0], color='teal', edgecolor='white')
axes[0].set_title('Average Demand by Hour of Day')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Hour')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Avg kWh')

dow_labels = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun']
df_agg.groupby('day_of_week')['total_kwh'].mean().plot(
    kind='bar', ax=axes[1], color='darkorange', edgecolor='white')
axes[1].set_title('Average Demand by Day of Week')
axes[1].set_xticklabels(dow_labels, rotation=0)
axes[1].set_ylabel('Avg kWh')

month_labels = ['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr','May','Jun','Jul','Aug','Sep','Oct','Nov','Dec']
df_agg.groupby('month')['total_kwh'].mean().plot(
    kind='bar', ax=axes[2], color='indianred', edgecolor='white')
axes[2].set_title('Average Demand by Month')
axes[2].set_xticklabels(month_labels, rotation=0)
axes[2].set_ylabel('Avg kWh')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

**Observations:**

- **Hour of day:** Double peak ~ A smaller morning peak around 7-9 AM and a larger evening peak around 5-9 PM with a deep trough in the overnight hours (~2-4 AM).
- **Day of week:** Weekends are only slightly higher than weekdays, as more people are home on the weekends during the day, but the lift is not significant.
- **Month:** A strong winter peak (Oct/Nov) driven by heating and lighting demand. This is balanced by a summer trough (Jun–Aug) but the net effect is dominated by the fact that demand for space heating far exceeds demand for space cooling.
Seasonal Demand Heatmap (Hour × Month)

pivot = df_agg.groupby(['month', 'hour_of_day'])['total_kwh'].mean().unstack()

month_labels = ['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr','May','Jun','Jul','Aug','Sep','Oct','Nov','Dec']

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6))
sns.heatmap(pivot, cmap='YlOrRd', yticklabels=month_labels, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Average Demand — Month × Hour of Day')
ax.set_xlabel('Hour of Day')
ax.set_ylabel('Month')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

**Observations:**

- it’s clear that the evening band affects all months fairly equally (~5–9 PM), but its magnitude increases dramatically in the winter months.
- It also is visible in the mornings of cold months as a heating load at wake-up time.
- This pattern is for a forecasting model to learn: both hour and month are relevant, and they are not independent.
Neighborhood Comparison

hourly_neigh = df_agg.groupby(['neighborhood', 'hour_of_day'])['total_kwh'].mean().reset_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 5))
for name, grp in hourly_neigh.groupby('neighborhood'):
    ax.plot(grp['hour_of_day'], grp['total_kwh'], marker='o', label=name)

ax.set_title('Average Hourly Demand Profile by Neighborhood')
ax.set_xlabel('Hour of Day')
ax.set_ylabel('Avg kWh')
ax.set_xticks(range(24))
ax.legend(title='Neighborhood', bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

**Observations:**

Note that all the ACORN neighbourhoods in the map have the same shape (i.e. they both have a morning and a evening peak) but differ greatly in magnitude.

Q1, Q3 = df_agg['total_kwh'].quantile([0.25, 0.75])

ax.axhline(upper, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)

ax.set_xlabel('Date')
ax.set_ylabel('kWh')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

**Observations:**

- Only a small percentage of rows are outside if the IQR bounds, also most of them appear to be extreme winder-evening demand spikes and not error. Therefore we retain these points.

df_weather['timestamp'] = pd.to_datetime(df_weather['time']).dt.floor('h')
df_weather = df_weather.drop_duplicates(subset='timestamp')

WEATHER_COLS = ['timestamp', 'temperature', 'humidity',
                'windSpeed', 'visibility', 'pressure', 'dewPoint']
df_weather = df_weather[WEATHER_COLS].rename(columns={
    'windSpeed': 'wind_speed',
    'dewPoint': 'dew_point',
})

for c in df_weather.columns.drop('timestamp'):
    df_weather[c] = pd.to_numeric(df_weather[c], errors='coerce').interpolate(limit=6)

df_merged = df_agg.merge(df_weather, on='timestamp', how='left')

Feature Engineering

We create five categories of features: | Category | Features | |----------|----------| | **Temporal** | hour, day_of_week, month, quarter, is_weekend, is_holiday | | **Lag** | demand at t−1, t−24, t−48, t−168 | | **Rolling** | 24h mean, 24h std, 7d mean | | **Weather** | temperature, humidity, wind, heating/cooling degree days | | **Derived** | peak_hour flag, temp×demand interaction |

def engineer_features(df):
    df = df.sort_values('timestamp').copy()

    df['hour']        = df['timestamp'].dt.hour
    df['day_of_week'] = df['timestamp'].dt.dayofweek
    df['month']       = df['timestamp'].dt.month
    df['is_weekend']  = (df['day_of_week'] >= 5).astype(int)

    df['hour_sin']  = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df['hour'] / 24)
    df['hour_cos']  = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df['hour'] / 24)
    df['month_sin'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df['month'] / 12)
    df['month_cos'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df['month'] / 12)

    for lag in [1, 24, 168]:
        df[f'lag_{lag}h'] = df['total_kwh'].shift(lag)

    df['rolling_24h_mean'] = df['total_kwh'].rolling(24, min_periods=12).mean()
    df['rolling_7d_mean']  = df['total_kwh'].rolling(168, min_periods=84).mean()

    base_temp = 18.0
    df['heating_degree'] = np.maximum(base_temp - df['temperature'], 0)
    df['cooling_degree'] = np.maximum(df['temperature'] - base_temp, 0)

    df['is_peak_hour'] = df['hour'].isin([7, 8, 9, 17, 18, 19, 20]).astype(int)
    return df

df_featured = (
    df_merged
    .groupby('neighborhood', group_keys=False)
    .apply(engineer_features)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

new_cols = [c for c in df_featured.columns if c not in df_merged.columns]
print(f"Feature-engineered dataset: {len(df_featured):,} rows × {len(df_featured.columns)} columns")
print(f"New columns ({len(new_cols)}): {new_cols}")

Several new features have been incorporated into the data, across 4 categories: calendar features (both raw and cyclical, sine and cosine encoded), lag features, (1 hour, 24 hours, 168 hours), rolling means (24 hours, 7 days), and weather-specific heating/cooling degrees. A peak hour flag has also been added to all days in the database.

def make_sequences(features, target, window, horizon):
    X, y = [], []
    for i in range(len(features) - window - horizon + 1):
        X.append(features[i : i + window])
        y.append(target[i + window : i + window + horizon].ravel())
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)

TCN Model

The model is a small stack of 1d convolution blocks with increasing dilation (1,2,4,8). Each block has a causal convolution (only left padded), ReLu activation and dropout. After the convolutional stack we average in time and predict the next 24 hours with a linear layer.

import copy

def train_model(model, train_loader, val_loader, epochs=20, lr=1e-3, patience=5):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()

    best_val = float('inf')
    best_state = None
    bad_epochs = 0
    history = {'train_loss': [], 'val_loss': []}

    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        train_loss = 0.0
        for xb, yb in train_loader:
            xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            pred = model(xb)
            loss = criterion(pred, yb)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            train_loss += loss.item() * xb.size(0)
        train_loss /= len(train_loader.dataset)

        model.eval()
        val_loss = 0.0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for xb, yb in val_loader:
                xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
                val_loss += criterion(model(xb), yb).item() * xb.size(0)
        val_loss /= len(val_loader.dataset)

        history['train_loss'].append(train_loss)
        history['val_loss'].append(val_loss)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch:02d} | train {train_loss:.4f} | val {val_loss:.4f}")

        if val_loss < best_val:
            best_val = val_loss
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
            bad_epochs = 0
        else:
            bad_epochs += 1
            if bad_epochs >= patience:
                print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch}")
                break

    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    return model, history


tcn_model, tcn_history = train_model(tcn_model, train_loader, val_loader, epochs=20, lr=1e-3)

plt.plot(tcn_history['val_loss'],   label='Validation')

Evaluate TCN on the Test Set

Predictions and actual values are inverse-scaled back to kWh before computing MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and R².

from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

def predict(model, loader):
    model.eval()
    preds, actuals = [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for xb, yb in loader:
            xb = xb.to(device)
            preds.append(model(xb).cpu().numpy())
            actuals.append(yb.numpy())
    return np.concatenate(preds), np.concatenate(actuals)


def evaluate(model, loader, name='Model'):
    pred_s, actual_s = predict(model, loader)
    pred   = target_scaler.inverse_transform(pred_s.reshape(-1, 1)).reshape(pred_s.shape)
    actual = target_scaler.inverse_transform(actual_s.reshape(-1, 1)).reshape(actual_s.shape)

    mae  = mean_absolute_error(actual.ravel(), pred.ravel())
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual.ravel(), pred.ravel()))
    mape = np.mean(np.abs((actual - pred) / np.clip(actual, 1e-3, None))) * 100
    r2   = r2_score(actual.ravel(), pred.ravel())

    print(f"{name}: MAE={mae:.3f} | RMSE={rmse:.3f} | MAPE={mape:.2f}% | R2={r2:.3f}")
    return {'name': name, 'MAE': mae, 'RMSE': rmse, 'MAPE': mape, 'R2': r2,
            'pred': pred, 'actual': actual}


tcn_results = evaluate(tcn_model, test_loader, name='TCN')

def plot_forecast(results, sample_idx=0, title=None):
    actual = results['actual'][sample_idx]
    pred   = results['pred'][sample_idx]
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
    plt.plot(actual, label='Actual', marker='o')
    plt.plot(pred,   label='Predicted', marker='x')
    plt.xlabel('Hour ahead'); plt.ylabel('Demand (kWh)')
    plt.title(title or f"{results['name']}: 24-hour forecast (sample {sample_idx})")
    plt.legend(); plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


plot_forecast(tcn_results, sample_idx=0)

import math

class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, max_len=5000):
        super().__init__()
        pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model)
        position = torch.arange(0, max_len).unsqueeze(1).float()
        div_term = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() *
                             (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model))
        pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * div_term)
        pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * div_term)
        self.register_buffer('pe', pe.unsqueeze(0))

    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.pe[:, :x.size(1)]


class TransformerForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features, horizon, d_model=64, nhead=4,
                 num_layers=2, dim_feedforward=128, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_proj = nn.Linear(n_features, d_model)
        self.pos_enc = PositionalEncoding(d_model)
        encoder_layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
            d_model=d_model, nhead=nhead,
            dim_feedforward=dim_feedforward,
            dropout=dropout, batch_first=True,
        )
        self.encoder = nn.TransformerEncoder(encoder_layer, num_layers=num_layers)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d_model, horizon)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.input_proj(x)
        x = self.pos_enc(x)
        x = self.encoder(x)
        x = x.mean(dim=1)
        return self.head(x)


tfm_model = TransformerForecaster(N_FEATURES, FORECAST_HORIZON).to(device)
print(tfm_model)
print(f"Trainable parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in tfm_model.parameters()):,}")

Train the Transformer

We use the same training loop as the TCN with a slightly smaller learning rate (1e-4), which is typical for Transformer training.

---

Conclusion

  • Both the TCN and the Transformer were trained with the same 168-hour input window to predict the next 24 hours of electricity demand for the primary neighbourhood.
  • The TCN trains quickly and performs well due to its dilated causal convolutions that already cover the full 1-week input window.
  • The self-attention in the Transformer directly models any past time step. It achieves comparable accuracy on this dataset with a small model (d_model=64, 2 layers).
  • The better model (lower MAE/RMSE and higher R 2 in the comparison table above) can be used for short term load forecasting for demand-response and grid optimisation in real smart-grid use.
